title: Harness Engineers, are you also here?
author: Altruistic-Spare9069
selftext:
Hello fellow game developers. While following this subs i've mostly observed a few types of posts:

* self promoting games
* people shocked about the frontier models possiblity trying to one-shot something that looks like a game
* hobbyst that work for years with passion wondering whether their game will be ai-slopped (called out as ai-slop)

Since the vibe-code is something different than harness engineering i'm wondering whether there are some people like me, that have a passion for games and years of experience in IT, maybe even working as AI Native Engineers and are experimenting with AI Native SDLC direction.

If you were inspired by articles like [https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) or others and you are developing your games using such approach, and not "just" prompt, observe, iterate until it works vibing please raise your hand  😄

comments.author: Short_Stable2397
comments.body: sooo instead of self promoting games you want us to self promote AI native software tools? I built an AI native MCP for Godot and a memory layer. Do they count? :P

replies.author: Altruistic-Spare9069
replies.body:
Hah well I'm not sure if I want anything, I'm just curious about your experiences. From my pespective working on something bigger that can't be finished in a few weekends requires a good plan, coordination, testing, documentation. While it seems that this is achievable with a permanent session agents well, its really hard to work like this. Constant context pollution, agent loosing context, contradict decisions and so on. At some point in time when I was working on my game I spent more and more tokens on things that stopped progressing, had hundreds of tests that were triggered too often and so on.   
At that time i've invested some time reorganizing process, how agents interact with each other and code base, how they get minimal amount of knowledge needed to do the task. It stopped my game development progress but gave me other type of satisfaction, seeing the improvement and in the long run hopefully , if not for my current project, then maybe for next one, it will be beneficial

replies.author: Short_Stable2397
replies.body:
yeah i hear you. I have a couple of games on the back burner where it is just so difficult to grind out because i'm not prompting well or the agent isn't on the same page as me. As a result i probably spend more time thinking about tooling than gamedev! i think it's all because of years spent as a developer.

i also have a forever project developing a custom harness and it's going about as well as you can imagine...

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
Yes, I think I’m in this camp. Although I enjoy making games I am also getting a lot out of learning how to use AI properly. This means putting a lot of effort into the environment my agents work within.

I don’t write or review any code myself. I’m used to that as my whole career has been on the non coder side of software development. What I do know is how to scope out work, keep a project on track and evaluate what has been created all while creating the processes around that.

replies.author: Altruistic-Spare9069
replies.body: The interesting part of AI native SDLC is that you don't review the code anymore, because you will be bottleneck. Instead you write boundaries, architecture and deterministic guardrails. For sure we are just doing baby steps for now as it is evolving constantly but it will be more obvious in short future

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
A lot of software development is very well documented. Thousands of articles exist on every aspect of the process and AI agents have access to almost all of it. Pure knowledge is not an edge.

Where we add value now is in filtering, combining and directing. The unique synthesis of our individual knowledge and experiences and the power to apply it at the right times.

For AI tools that means building a system that reflects our own views of the process so we can run it with minimum friction. It means you don’t have to compromise with colleagues who have different philosophies but also you own all of the consequences.

replies.author: Altruistic-Spare9069
replies.body: That's what i'm talking about, tooling is one of the most necessary things in the puzzle. I've played around comfy-ui and some sdl like Juggernaut or Trellis2 and it seems that the most difficult part is rigging /animation.

replies.author: Fulgren09
replies.body: The big insight I had for animation was to use 6th gen console techniques, which is make every polygon do double duty as both 'visual' and 'gameplay'. Its much more tractable to get LLM to rig a PS2/Gamecube looking character with just three.js and Blender. Much quicker to figure out "is this game loop interesting?"

comments.author: egonosz
comments.body:
10+ years game programmer here. I am working on pretty complex AA games with many interdependent systems. I personally specialise on architecture and optimisation. 

I working on my custom engine for fun, the goals are high performance(maximum parallelism) and simple to write safe code.

My harness is pretty simple:  
I have verify.bat which accepts parameters for verification.(which target, tests, usan, asan, etc.)  
In my agent.md, short brief of the repo, where are the docs and how to verify the work. Not more than 200 words.  
I have five different documentation types, all of them have an index and multiple files:  
Architecture files have the high level description of a system and decided limits.  
Features have the description or more complex features.  
To-do files well self explanatory.  
How-to files (I found the most useful), is description of how to do things, like write documentation, create a new “game object”, create files etc. 

This is my setup + the engine what I am working on has architecture which is human and ai friendly( minimal amount of inheritance, highly data oriented and you cannot make easily multithreading mistakes).

Now I read all the code and fix  what the ai spits out. For architectural decisions (like how should the asset management look), first I figure out what/how/why (so I do not get biased by ai and after I ask it. The reason for this flow is that if you ask the AI to plan you an asset management system it will just spits out the unity or ue one.

I am not vibe coder, but this rule may help them too:  
Plan and let ai implement only that what you actually need for your next step. Do not let it implement things which you may need, it is way easier to do this with AI, because it can interpret conversation as request.  
Read the plan!

I hope this will help someone, no fancy MCP on my side(yet).

comments.author: siberianmi
comments.body:
I’ve been in IT in various roles for… oh god, 30 years now.

I’ve been having more fun with computers than probably anytime in my career over the last few years thanks to AI.  My day to day job has shifted into helping others apply AI and building tools to enable that.

I’ve dabbled a bit with AI for game development and for me recently the big unlock was how well AI plus Godot can build with voxels.  I have it building real smoke tests along the way that already have found bugs in the procedural generation system for the game world.  Last night I had it build a preview mode tool so I can iterate more easily with it in individual game assets where it’s code changes are reflected live.

It’ll probably never see the light of day but I’m having fun.
